meta.title: Who originally recorded "Tennessee Waltz"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Patti Page's 1950 smash was a cover. Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys recorded "Tennessee Waltz" in 1947 and RCA Victor released it in January 1948.
meta.ogDescription: Not Patti Page. Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys cut it on 2 December 1947; RCA Victor issued it in January 1948, a No. 3 country hit.

answer.label: Not a Patti Page original — a 1948 Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys single on RCA Victor
answer.originalArtist: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
answer.originalArtistDates: Pee Wee King, 1914–2000 · American country bandleader and songwriter; the Golden West Cowboys were his Grand Ole Opry band
answer.sourceLine: Patti Page’s 1950 record is so total a possession of this song that most people assume she introduced it. She did not. “Tennessee Waltz” was written in 1946 by bandleader Pee Wee King and his singer Redd Stewart, and King’s Golden West Cowboys cut it on 2 December 1947 at RCA Victor’s Chicago studio; RCA Victor issued it as single 20-2680 on 26 January 1948, and it reached No. 3 country. Page’s Mercury version arrived in November 1950 and spent nine weeks at No. 1 on the pop chart — and the country original has been standing in its shadow ever since.

trail: The 1948 single is catalogued as Victor 20-2680, and a transfer of the shellac itself is preserved at the Internet Archive ↗.
Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ gives the 2 December 1947 session, the 26 January 1948 release, and the No. 3 country placing.
A second pre-Page version exists: Cowboy Copas cut it for King Records in March 1948, reaching No. 6 country — documented in the same Wikipedia entry ↗.
The composition, registered by Acuff-Rose in February 1948, is credited on MusicBrainz ↗ to Pee Wee King as composer and Redd Stewart as lyricist.

authors.name: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
authors.heading: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
authors.metaLine: Pee Wee King, 1914–2000 · American country bandleader · recorded 2 December 1947, released January 1948 on RCA Victor
authors.bio: Born Julius Frank Anthony Kuczynski in Abrams, Wisconsin, Pee Wee King led the Golden West Cowboys, one of the most stylistically adventurous bands ever to work the Grand Ole Opry — he pushed waltzes, polkas and cowboy material into country music, and his band brought stage dancing and rhinestone tailoring to the Opry stage. He wrote or co-wrote more than 400 songs and cut more than 150 singles. His Golden West Cowboys recorded “Tennessee Waltz” on 2 December 1947 for RCA Victor; the single reached No. 3 on the country chart and sold some 300,000 copies. King was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1974.

authors.name: Patti Page
authors.heading: Patti Page
authors.metaLine: 1927–2013 · American pop singer · Mercury single, November 1950 · nine weeks at No. 1
authors.bio: Clara Ann Fowler of Claremore, Oklahoma became the top-charting female vocalist of the 1950s and one of the first pop artists to harmonise with herself on record, via engineer Bill Putnam’s overdubbing. Her “Tennessee Waltz” reached her almost by accident: Billboard reviewer Jerry Wexler heard an R&B version by Erskine Hawkins and suggested the song to Page’s manager Jack Rael, and it was cut in a hurry as the flip of a Christmas novelty. It spent nine weeks at No. 1 and became one of the best-selling singles of the century. Nothing about that record is a mistake — only the chronology people attach to it.

authors.name: Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart
authors.heading: Pee Wee King & Redd Stewart
authors.metaLine: Pee Wee King, 1914–2000 · Redd Stewart, 1923–2003 · written 1946 · published by Acuff-Rose Music
authors.bio: King and Stewart wrote “Tennessee Waltz” in 1946, on the road to Nashville, after hearing Bill Monroe’s “Kentucky Waltz” and deciding their own state deserved one. Henry Ellis “Redd” Stewart, born in Ashland City, Tennessee, had joined the Golden West Cowboys in 1937 and became the band’s lead singer after Eddy Arnold went solo; he also wrote “Soldier’s Last Letter,” a 1944 hit for Ernest Tubb, and co-wrote “You Belong to Me” with King. Because the writers were also the first recording act, this page’s correction is unusually clean: the men who made the record made the song.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong beginning
misattribution.intro: Patti Page’s record is one of the best-selling singles of the twentieth century, which is exactly why it is mistaken for the first one. Here is the order things actually happened in.

items.who: Patti Page originated “Tennessee Waltz” with her 1950 Mercury single.
items.why: Her version spent nine weeks at No. 1 on the pop chart and had sold 2.3 million copies by May 1951, dwarfing everything that came before it in the mainstream market.

items.who: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys, recorded 2 December 1947, released by RCA Victor as 20-2680 on 26 January 1948.
items.why: It reached No. 3 on the country chart and sold around 300,000 copies — a substantial country hit that never reached the pop audience Page later did.
Copas’s cover reached No. 6 country and sold about 80,000 copies, meaning the song had been a hit twice over before Page ever sang it.

items.who: Pee Wee King (music) and Redd Stewart (lyrics), written in 1946.
items.why: Unusually, the writers were also the first recording act — King led the band and Stewart was its lead singer — so the credit and the origin point at the same people.

misattribution.truthLine: First recorded by Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys, 2 December 1947; released on RCA Victor in January 1948. Patti Page’s version came in November 1950.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question is not why Patti Page had a hit — it is why a record that had already been a country hit twice could be treated, in 1950, as brand new. The answer is that in the late 1940s the country chart and the pop chart described two more or less sealed markets. Pee Wee King’s RCA Victor single went to No. 3 country in 1948 and Cowboy Copas’s King Records version followed it to No. 6, but neither crossed into the pop audience that bought Mercury singles.

The bridge was accidental. Billboard reviewer Jerry Wexler — years before Atlantic Records made him famous — heard an R&B version by Erskine Hawkins in October 1950 and passed the song to Page’s manager Jack Rael. Page cut it fast, without a proper arrangement, as the B-side of a Christmas novelty. The novelty is forgotten; the flip side spent nine weeks at No. 1 and sold in the millions. When a record outsells its predecessors by that margin, the public files it as the beginning of the story.
detailsBody: 1946 — Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart write “Tennessee Waltz,” prompted by Bill Monroe’s “Kentucky Waltz.”
2 December 1947 — Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys record it at RCA Victor Studio A in Chicago.
26 January 1948 — RCA Victor issues the single as Victor 20-2680; it reaches No. 3 on the country chart and sells about 300,000 copies.
26 February 1948 — the composition is registered by Acuff-Rose Publications of Nashville.
March 1948 — Cowboy Copas releases a competing version on King Records 696, reaching No. 6 country.
October 1950 — Billboard’s Jerry Wexler reviews an Erskine Hawkins R&B version and recommends the song to Patti Page’s manager, Jack Rael.
November 1950 — Page’s Mercury single (catalogue 5534) appears with “Tennessee Waltz” as the flip of “Boogie Woogie Santa Claus.”
30 December 1950 — Page’s version reaches No. 1 on the Billboard pop chart, where it stays for nine weeks; it had sold 2.3 million copies by May 1951.
1965 — Tennessee adopts the song as an official state song by Senate Joint Resolution 9.
context.pull: The song was a country hit twice before America heard it.
